title: Feed Milling Process Control and Automation

lessons.title: Control systems in a modern feed mill
lessons.html:
Control systems in a modern feed mill

Most commercial feed mills in South Africa run on automated control systems. The operator works from a control room, starting routes, launching batches and watching alarms. Understanding the system makes the difference between an operator who reacts and one who controls the process.

Layers of control

LayerFunction
Field devicesSensors (load cells, level probes, temperature probes, speed sensors, flow meters) and actuators (motors, slide gates, diverters, valves)
PLC (programmable logic controller)Runs the logic: starts and stops equipment, interlocks, batching sequences
SCADA / HMIScreens showing the plant, alarms, trends; operators give commands here
Batch and ERP softwareFormulations, production orders, stock, traceability records

Routes and interlocks

A route is a path material takes, for example from intake pit 1 via elevator 2 and distributor position 5 into silo 3. The system starts equipment in reverse order (downstream first) so material always has somewhere to go, and stops it in forward order (upstream first) so lines run empty.

Interlocks prevent unsafe or wrong operation: an elevator cannot start if its downstream conveyor is stopped; a mixer cannot discharge if the surge bin below is full; a gate cannot open to a bin allocated to a different ingredient. Interlocks must never be bypassed without formal authorisation and a risk assessment.

Batching automation

The batch controller takes the formulation, calculates target weights per batch, opens bin feeders, weighs each ingredient (often with fast and slow feed rates to reduce overshoot), records actual weights, and holds or alarms when a weight is out of tolerance. Hand-add stations for micro-ingredients often use barcode scanning so the system confirms the correct premix is added.

lessons.title: Control loops, alarms and data
lessons.html:
Control loops, alarms and data

Closed-loop control

Some processes are controlled continuously. In a closed loop, a sensor measures the process value, the controller compares it with the set point and adjusts an output.

  • Conditioner temperature: the controller opens or closes the steam valve to hold the set temperature.
  • Pellet mill load: feeder speed is adjusted to keep main motor current near a target, maximising throughput without choking.
  • Cooler: discharge rate or airflow adjusted to hold product temperature.

Most such loops use PID control (proportional, integral, derivative). Poorly tuned loops oscillate or respond slowly; tuning is done by competent technicians, not by trial and error during production.

Alarm management

  • Alarms have priorities. High-priority alarms, such as a choked elevator or high bin level, need immediate action.
  • Acknowledge, diagnose and act; never silence repeating alarms without finding the cause.
  • Too many nuisance alarms lead operators to ignore real ones. Report nuisance alarms so they can be reviewed.

Data and traceability

Automation records what happened: batch weights, times, operator, ingredient lots, process temperatures and downtime. This data supports traceability, cost control and problem solving. Trends help spot gradual problems such as die wear (rising amps per tonne) or scale drift.

Calibration and reliability

  • Load cells and flow meters are calibrated on schedule with certified test weights or methods.
  • Temperature probes are checked against a reference.
  • Back up PLC programs and formulation databases.
  • Control access with passwords so only authorised staff change set points or recipes, and log changes.
  • Plan for power interruptions: safe shutdown sequences, UPS for controllers, and restart checks.

Key points

  • Field devices, PLC, SCADA and batch software form the control system.
  • Routes start downstream first and stop upstream first.
  • Interlocks must never be bypassed without authorisation.
  • Closed loops hold conditioner temperature and pellet mill load.
  • Respond to alarms properly and keep instruments calibrated.
  • Control access to set points and recipes and log changes.
